implementation_notes: `lazy var` is part of the language (the Properties chapter of The Swift Programming Language): the initializer does not run at instance creation but on the first read, and the result is stored. Type-level lazy state comes for free as well - a `static let` is initialized on first access by the runtime, which is the dispatch_once-style guard you would otherwise hand-write - and it is immutable. Lazy stored properties must be var (`lazy let` does not compile) because the value is written after initialization, which also means a struct's lazy property can only be read through a mutable instance. There is no way to invalidate a lazy var: for a resource that must be closed or refreshed, keep an Optional and acquire inside a method so the owner can set it back to nil.
pitfalls: A lazy instance property carries no synchronization guarantee, unlike static let/global storage that the runtime initializes atomically: two threads can both observe the uninitialized state and run the initializer twice, so a shared object's lazily acquired resource needs an explicit guard.

Reading a lazy property mutates the instance: from a `let` struct value the compiler reports 'cannot use mutating getter on immutable value', which surprises code that treats the accessor as a pure read.

A lazy property is one-shot: after first access it is just a stored property, and the declared initializer can never re-run; assigning a value before first access suppresses the initializer, so release or re-acquisition needs an Optional plus a method.

A lazy initializer that captures self keeps a strong reference for the lifetime of the instance and is a common retain-cycle source, so capture self weakly when the acquired object can outlive its owner.
